title: Optimize walkthrough — batching & prefix/KV cache cost model with Verdigris Robotics
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran an Optimize-focused walkthrough covering batching, KV/prefix prefetch strategies, and a cost model tailored to Verdigris Robotics' conversational telemetry use-case. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, encryption/KMS concerns for session caching, and next steps to run a 72-hour pilot and provide a cost-sensitivity spreadsheet.
topics: Cost model and sensitivity to latency and QPS
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment
Security: KMS, audit logs, data retention
next_steps: Redwood: Share cost-sensitivity spreadsheet + sample console export
Customer: Provide 24-hour sample traffic trace and top-10 prompt families
Redwood SE: Run a 72-hour pilot with 2k-10k QPS synthetic mix on dedicated pool
Schedule follow-up technical deep dive to validate KV TTL settings (target 2026-02-27)
action_items: Priya Nair - prepare cost-sensitivity model and send by 2026-02-23
Ethan Cole - upload 24h traffic sample to shared S3 link by 2026-02-22
Miguel Santos - configure pilot cluster and provide runbook by 2026-02-25
Samira Patel - confirm security reviewer availability for SOC2/ISO chat by 2026-02-26
meeting_header:
Date: 2026-02-20 | Start: 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~68 minutes
Redwood: Alex Chen, Priya Nair, Miguel Santos | Verdigris Robotics: Samira Patel, Ethan Cole, Jordan Lee, Nadia Kaur
transcript:
00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Um we're gonna run through the Optimize playbook focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations for your conversational agents. I think we have 60-70 mins scheduled, so we'll go a little deep on the cost model.
01:20 Samira Patel: Thanks Alex. Quick context — our prod traffic right now is mostly dialogue sessions from customer support bots, average session length 9 turns, token footprint around 1.2k tokens per session. Peak concurrency hits about 650 concurrent users, typical avg QPS ~45.
02:05 Priya Nair: Got it. That average session length is helpful. One thing we'll look at: how much you can save by sessionization + prefix caching on the KV cache and what batching looks like under your latency SLOs.
03:10 Jordan Lee: Our latency budget is pretty strict — p95 end-to-end needs to be under 700ms. How does batching not blow that up?
03:45 Priya Nair: Good question. Two levers — continuous batching with adaptive time windows, and aggressive prefix/KV caching so many requests short-circuit the full decode path. We can tune batch sizes to keep p95 under your SLO while still improving throughput.
05:02 Ethan Cole: Can you explain prefix cache again? We looked at docs but terms got mixed. Is it like a prompt cache or more of a KV key for the attention cache?
05:30 Miguel Santos: Sure — sorry our docs sometimes say prefix cache, sometimes KV cache, and you might see 'session KV' or 'prefetch'. They all map to the same idea: we store the model's KV (key/value) state for shared prefixes so subsequent continuations avoid re-computing the prefix. For dialogue that's super effective because the system prompt + history is reused.
06:22 Samira Patel: And how long do those keys live? Our compliance folks worry about storing customer text in cache.
06:40 Alex Chen: TTL is configurable. Typical patterns: session-level TTL (e.g., 30–120 minutes) or explicit evict on logout. For regulated data you can encrypt keys at rest and use KMS/HSM integration — Redwood's Private deployment supports customer-managed KMS. On hosted we offer envelope encryption and configurable retention policies.
07:35 Nadia Kaur: So what's the expected cost delta between no-caching vs prefix cache at our profile?
08:00 Priya Nair: I'll do a simplified back-of-envelope now: assume 45 QPS, avg 1.2k tokens per session, and 9-turn sessions. If you can cache 60% of the prefix tokens with KV hits, you save ~45-55% of decode time for those requests — but actual token cost depends on hit rate and batch efficiency. We'll show a spreadsheet after.
09:20 Alex Chen: We're also going to show tradeoffs with batching — as you increase batch window you get better token-per-second throughput but higher tail latency. For your 700ms p95, we typically cap batching windows to 40-60ms and rely on fast-path cache hits to keep tails low.
10:40 Jordan Lee: Do you have metrics from similar customers? Something like before/after numbers?
11:05 Priya Nair: Yes — for a convo use-case with 8 turn average, we saw ~48% cost reduction from combined sessionization + KV prefetch, and p95 improved because cached hits avoid long decodes. But if you have very high variability or long prefixes, hit rate drops.
12:30 Ethan Cole: On the dedicated pool — how predictable is throughput? We want reserved capacity for peak, but don't want to overcommit.
13:00 Miguel Santos: Dedicated is explicit GPU pools: you commit to a capacity and get predictable throughput and option for burst capacity. For predictable economics we can recommend target vGPU units based on your 95th percentile QPS and desired headroom. We included autoscale policies that can be tuned to keep cost down while meeting peaks.
14:22 Samira Patel: Are there configuration knobs we need to change in the console? Like the model variant, quantization, kernel selection?
14:40 Priya Nair: Yes — Optimize in the console will give suggested quantization and model variants. For instance, switching to a q4f16 profile at certain seq lengths can cut cost but may slightly affect quality. We'll flag model variants as compatible fallbacks in case of capacity constraints.
15:55 Alex Chen: Let's walk a short example with your traffic shape. Ethan, you mentioned 9-turn sessions, can you describe the prompt families? Are some prompts long system messages?
16:22 Ethan Cole: Yeah we have 3 primary families: quick FAQ replies (~200 tokens), guided troubleshooting (~800 tokens), and ticket summarization (~2k tokens but rare). Most traffic is the FAQ and troubleshooting.
17:05 Priya Nair: That helps — caching will be most effective on the FAQ + mid-size troubleshooting since those share stable system prompts. For the ticket summarization, batching may help but cache hit rate will be low.
18:10 Jordan Lee: What about prefetch? Do you precompute the KV for the next expected turn? That seems risky if users branch off.
18:40 Miguel Santos: Prefetch is heuristic — we can prefetch likely next tokens for deterministic flows. For highly branching dialog you might prefetch the top-k continuations or only warm the KV for the system prompt portion. There's a cost/benefit tradeoff; our Optimize tool simulates expected savings based on your trace.
20:00 Samira Patel: Okay show us the console then?
20:15 Alex Chen: Sure — sharing screen now — (brief pause) — you can see the Optimize dashboard, suggestions panel on the right, and a cost-sensitivity slider. We can import your sample traffic and run an estimated saving sim.
21:40 Priya Nair: Here's a sample run we prepared using a synthetic mix approximating your distribution: 60% FAQ, 35% troubleshooting, 5% long summarization. The simulation projects a 39-52% delta in token decode spend depending on TTL and hit-rate assumptions.
23:15 Ethan Cole: What assumptions are baked into that sim? Hit rate distribution? Batch size?
23:40 Priya Nair: The sim assumes a base hit rate of 0.62 for prefixes, batch window 50ms, concurrency 650 in peak, and quantized model q4f16. We provide knobs to vary each parameter and see the sensitivity.
25:05 Jordan Lee: Let's talk about tail latency outliers — we can't accept 99.9th being multi-second. What mitigations are there?
25:30 Miguel Santos: Several: keep small max batching window, enforce fast-path route for cache hits, model fallbacks (smaller model variant) for tail requests, and regional routing to avoid noisy neighbours. Also, KV cache hits are typically an order magnitude faster because they skip prefix decode.
27:10 Samira Patel: On security — we need SSO + SAML for console access and detailed audit logs for the pilot. Do you export audit logs to our SIEM?
27:35 Alex Chen: Yes — we support SAML SSO and can stream audit logs (or provide daily exports). For Private deployments you can Retain logs inside your VPC. We also have per-token attribution in the console so you can map costs to teams.
29:00 Nadia Kaur: For token accounting, how do you measure tokenization differences? Our tokenizer isn't always the same across models.
29:30 Priya Nair: Good point. Our model catalog shows tokenizer metrics per model. The cost sim normalizes to tokens as Redwood counts them in the runtime; if you need exact parity we can run your tokenizer against sample prompts during the pilot.
31:00 Ethan Cole: If we do a 72-hour pilot on dedicated, what's the minimum footprint?
31:20 Miguel Santos: Minimum recommended is a small reserved pool that reflects your p95 peak: for your 650 concurrency and 45 QPS avg, we'd likely start with two A100-equivalent groups (we map to Redwood vGPU units) — exact sizing we'll model and propose. The pilot will instrument KV hit rates and latency under real routing.
33:10 Samira Patel: Can we limit caching so customer PII isn't stored? Like mask or redact?
33:40 Alex Chen: Yes — we support redaction at ingestion or token-level filtering before storing KV. Also customer-managed KMS lets you ensure keys are yours. We can provide a security artifact that explains retention, encryption, and audit capabilities.
35:00 Priya Nair: Back to cost model: I'll show a quick sensitivity chart — (screen) — x-axis is KV hit rate, y-axis is total inference spend. At low hit rates (<30%) benefits are limited; at >50% you get steep savings. There's also a curve for batching — larger batch windows increase throughput savings but flatten quickly due to latency constraints.
37:10 Jordan Lee: Hypothetically, if hit rate is only 30% and we have to keep TTL short, what's the fallback? Do we still get some benefits?
37:35 Priya Nair: Yes, you'll still benefit from batching and quantization. Also you can target specific prompt families for caching — even a partial hit on high-cost prompts helps. The Optimize console allows you to annotate prompt families so caching is selective.
39:00 Ethan Cole: Anything we should be aware of integration-wise? SDK changes or header propagation?
39:20 Miguel Santos: Minimal — we have a small SDK header to enable sessionization and attach session IDs so KV keys align. If you use our HTTP API you pass session_id and optionally hint tags for prompt family. For streaming, we support early commit of the prefix KV.
41:05 Samira Patel: Can we throttle per-customer? We have enterprise accounts that need higher priority.
41:20 Alex Chen: Yes — policy routing in Redwood allows per-tenant priority, reserved throughput, and cost attribution. You can also pin high-tier tenants to dedicated slices.
42:10 Nadia Kaur: Competitors — are there any features they do better? We looked at Anthropic and some homegrown runtimes.
42:30 Priya Nair: Competitors might have stronger model ecosystems or close cloud integrations; what we focus on is the production inference ergonomics — the automatic simulations, recommended TTLs/quant profiles, and unified routing across hosted/dedicated/private. Also our Evaluate/Optimize link helps guard quality regressions when changing quant or model variants.
44:00 Ethan Cole: Can we see a sample of the cost-sensitivity spreadsheet?
44:20 Alex Chen: We'll send a spreadsheet after the call. It includes scenarios for hit rates, batch windows, model variants, and dedicated vs hosted pricing.
45:05 Miguel Santos: Quick note on measuring KV hit rate during pilot — instrument should log per-request whether it was a full decode, cache hit, or fallback. We'll include that metric in the dashboard.
46:10 Samira Patel: For the pilot, we'll need an NDA addendum and the security pack.
46:25 Alex Chen: Noted — I'll get legal to attach the pilot addendum and security pack.
47:10 Jordan Lee: Any known degradation in output quality from q4f16 quant? We care about hallucination on summaries.
47:40 Priya Nair: Small regressions are possible; we run SxA evals on your prompt set in the pilot to surface quality deltas. For summaries we often keep a higher-precision variant or run a rescoring pass.
49:00 Ethan Cole: Can you remind us of the typical savings ranges seen by customers of our size?
49:20 Priya Nair: For mid-market convo-heavy customers with similar distribution: 30-55% savings depending on hit rate and model choices. For very stable prefixes savings can exceed 60%.
50:10 Samira Patel: Ok let's recap next steps — who takes what?
50:25 Alex Chen: Recap — Redwood will: 1) send cost-sensitivity spreadsheet (Priya), 2) configure pilot and run a 72-hour test (Miguel), 3) share security pack and pilot addendum (Alex/legal). Verdigris: upload 24h traffic trace (Ethan), confirm security reviewer (Samira).
51:40 Nadia Kaur: Timeline — can we aim for pilot start in the week of Feb 24th?
51:55 Miguel Santos: Yes that's feasible if we get the trace and NDA signed this week.
53:00 Ethan Cole: One last nit — your SDK header examples, do they have code in TypeScript?
53:15 Miguel Santos: Yes we'll include SDK snippets for TS and Python in the follow-up.
54:20 Samira Patel: Great — thanks everyone.
54:30 Alex Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and a calendar invite for the pilot planning session.
54:50 (call ends)
transcription_notes: Occasional mis-hearings: product name 'Optimize' sometimes transcribed as 'Optimizer'; KV sometimes written as 'K V' or 'K-V'. Some timestamps approximate. Conversation contains typical sales cadence: qualification, demo, security concerns, next steps.
